title: Fed by ravens (1 Kings 17:1–7)
hook: Elijah hides by a brook, and ravens bring bread and meat

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kingdom splits, and a young king who set aside the old men's counsel. Your line was listen to the old ones. Did you ask an elder something real? Day seven hundred thirty.

Bread and meat, twice a day, delivered by birds. That's where today goes, but it starts with a man walking into the story out of nowhere. No birth story, no call. Just a name, Elijah the Tishbite, of Gilead, and a sentence to the king of Israel, Ahab: "As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word." Then, just as suddenly, the word comes to Elijah: get out of here. Turn east. Hide yourself by the brook Cherith, near the Jordan. Today, fed by ravens.

Here's the promise Elijah is given, in the King James Bible: "thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there." And the text says he simply went, and did it. Then the line that gives the story its name: "the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook." Three things are worth slowing down for. First, the delivery service. In the law of Moses, the raven appears on the list of birds Israel was not to eat: "Every raven after his kind." So the bread for God's prophet comes in the beak of a bird his own law kept off the table. The help arrives from an unexpected quarter. Second, Elijah has to receive it. A man who has just faced down a king now sits by a stream and waits for birds. There's no way to earn this meal, only to be there when it comes. Third, it doesn't last. "And it came to pass after a while, that the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land." The drought Elijah announced reaches him too. The ravens were for a season, not forever, and tomorrow's story begins because the water ran out. Much later, Jesus points at the same birds when he talks about worry. In Luke's Gospel he says: "Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them." Some readers hear the two passages together: the bird that is fed, and the bird that feeds a prophet.
screen: `AFTER A WHILE, THE BROOK DRIED UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let something unlikely feed you. Settle, and breathe. Think back to help you got from a source you'd never have chosen: a stranger, someone you didn't much like, a setback that turned out to carry something. Then look at today. Is there help being offered right now that you've been too proud, or too wary, to take? Don't decide what to do about it yet. Just let yourself picture receiving it. If you pray, you can give thanks for one raven in your life. The bell holds the time.
Fed by ravens. Hidden by a brook in a drought, Elijah is kept alive by birds, morning and evening, until the water runs out.
Your line: the ravens came. Today, say yes to one bit of help you'd normally wave away, from whoever it comes. Day seven hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Elijah and the ravens as a picture of God's daily provision, and the story is sometimes paired with Jesus's words about the ravens in Luke 12 when churches teach about worry.

original.note: Hebrew: ravens, the birds commanded to feed Elijah (1 Kings 17:4, 17:6).

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet story about birds bringing a picnic.
what it means: a hiding prophet in a drought, kept alive for a while by birds, until the brook runs dry.
what a scholar hears: the raven is on the law's list of birds not to eat (Leviticus 11:15), and Jesus later says, consider the ravens (Luke 12:24).
